For SKSC individuals with a gold standard variant in an established KSD gene, we looked at the Exomiser ranking of the respective gene based on its phenotype and variant scoring. As part of the variant-level scoring, we used the following algorithms for in silico variant pathogenicity prediction: MVP, REVEL, AlphaMissense, and SpliceAI, as recommended by a previous optimization study for rare diseases (33). The MAF cutoff for disregarding variants which are too common in the general population to be of interest remained at the default setting of 2% for compound heterozygous models and was raised from 0.1% to 1% for autosomal dominant and recessive -homozygous alternative models. The exact prevalence of monogenic KSD in the general population remains uncertain. However, we considered 1% as an approximate estimate, considering KSD general population prevalence of ~ 10% (34) and ~ 10% of KSD to be monogenic. The latter estimate is based on our previous study with 6.7% of the SKSC identified as monogenic (21), allowing for some additional missed cases. Furthermore, variants ranking top 1 in > 10% of the SKSC sample were disregarded, given the high false positive likelihood. Everything ranking below them was ranked up +1 to compensate.

We estimated the performance of each Exomiser run by calculating the proportion of gold standard variants in established genes (21), using increasing rank thresholds from 1 to 30.

We did not consider variants with rank above 30 since this was adding too much noise to the results, in line with Exomiser optimization research in rare diseases (33). The variant prioritization was considered to be successful if the previously established gene was prioritized by Exomiser in the same individual, regardless of the specific variant and mode of inheritance (MOI), i.e., gene-level success.

In our initial analysis, the previously identified gold standard variant was identified by Exomiser within the top 30 rankings in 63 % (N = 32) of carriers. To optimize Exomiser's performance, we successively re-ran the analyses with the following setting alterations:

Expanding the list of phenotypes Multiple phenotypes (HPO codes) can be provided to Exomiser for the same individual and broadening the search by extending the phenotype list can be beneficial in certain cases.

Therefore, an expert nephrologist provided a list of terms biologically linked to nephrolithiasis (e.g., hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, etc.) which were then mapped onto HPO codes (Suppl. Table 2), N = 31. When multiple HPO codes were available, the most general one was selected.

2) Disregarding the mode of inheritance

Exomiser uses OMIM inheritance mode information by checking if a patient's candidate genotype is consistent with the reported disease inheritance pattern and halves the phenotype score in case of inconsistency. As previously mentioned, the mode of inheritance for our "gold standard" variants did not always align with what is reported in OMIM for the respective established gene. This is due to the "gold standard" utilizing an additional level of information -blood and urine biochemistry data. For example, SLC34A3 is listed only under autosomal recessive inheritance in OMIM, while it was identified as autosomal dominant in our "gold standard" list and confirmed by other cohorts (50, 51). Given the very recent publication of this list, it has not yet been incorporated in OMIM. Therefore, we reran Exomiser disregarding the OMIM inheritance mode contribution to the scoring.

As indicated above, when focusing on the first 30 ranked genes per participant and selecting "nephrolithiasis" as the only phenotype Exomiser found the previously established variants in 63% (N = 32) of cases. When focusing only on the first one or the first five top-ranked genes with default values, we identified 59% (N = 30), and 63% (N = 32) carriers, respectively (Figure 2A). With the optimized pipeline, extending the phenotype list and disregarding inheritance mode, 94% (N = 48) of the variants were identified within the top 5 ranks.

Including variants further down the list did not substantially improve performance beyond rank 5. Only 1 additional carrier was identified when extending to rank <= 30, reaching a total of 96% (49 out of 51 carriers prioritized).

The two unidentified gene-participant pairings were for the genes SLC4A1 and SLC34A3, respectively. In the case of SLC4A1, this was due to the variant (c.713A>T) having a GnomAD MAF slightly above the set threshold. The missed variant in SLC34A3 (c.1058G>T) was filtered out due to a variant score of 0.76. Given that this was the only "gold standard" variant with variant score below our set threshold of 0.8 (Figure 2B), we decided not to lower the threshold to avoid introducing noise when extending to novel genes.

As all gold standard variants had a phenotype score > 0.5 (Figure 2B), we decided to increase our initially set threshold of 0.2 to 0.5 for this metric. The majority of the gold standard variants were assigned as variants of unknown significance (VUS) by the automated Exomiser assignment (Figure 2C), indicating that the addition of clinical data (in this case biochemical data relevant for the analyzed genes) improves variant classification as expected.

Nominating candidate novel kidney stone genes

After having used the previous gold standard dataset to optimize Exomiser in this context and ensuring that it successfully prioritizes the majority of manually found established KSD genes with clinically relevant variants, we next moved towards nominating novel candidate genes for monogenic forms of KSD among genes not associated with KSD yet. Considering our large sample size, we focused only on variants with rank 1, for noise reduction.

We used the following filtering criteria when evaluating putative novel KSD genes: a)

Variants within a gene must be present in at least two cases.; b) A variant can be present in no more than 1% of cases or controls.; c) The odds ratio for a given gene is > 0.25 (to remove genes where the odds of carrying a variant within that gene are substantially higher in controls than in cases: this filtering step removes obvious negatives but keeps genes with, e.g., 1 carrier in cases and 1 in controls to avoid being too stringent, as controls may have a relevant variant with incomplete penetrance and/or develop a KS later in life).; d) The variant carrier was filtered out if the individual was also a carrier of a gold standard variant in an established KSD gene (i.e. already had a monogenic cause identified); e) The variant should not be classified as (likely) benign by Exomiser's automated ACMG criteria assignment.

Using this optimized pipeline, we identified 62 genes as novel candidates for KSD. A list of all identified genes can be found in Suppl. Table 3, and more detailed information regarding the variants identified (N total = 176: 159 VUS; 16 LP; 1 P, as assigned by Exomiser) and their carriers (including urine and blood biochemistry) is available per gene from our online browser: https://sksc-variant-and-biochemistry.shinyapps.io/exomiser-candidates/. Based on gene-set overrepresentation analysis, we found these genes to be predominantly involved in purine nucleotide metabolic process (GO:0006163) and in monoatomic cation homeostasis (GO:0055080) (Figure 3A). 49 of the 62 genes nominated by Exomiser already have an OMIM-recorded disease association while 13 have not yet been described as monogenic disease genes. Among the 49 candidate genes known to be associated with other non-KSD diseases, we identified ATP7B, FGF23, GNA11 and PHEX, which have already been associated to some extent with KSD and are already included in some, but not all, KSD genetic testing panels (52). FGF23 and GNA11 for example are also included in the Genomics England PanelApp for nephrocalcinosis or nephrolithiasis as candidate "red" genes, i.e., genes with low level of evidence -supported by a single source or only preliminary data (v6.3; https://panelapp.genomicsengland.co.uk/panels/149/ (39)).

Similarly, ATP7B or CFTR cause distinct disorders (Wilson disease and cystic fibrosis respectively), where some evidence of association with kidney stones has been previously reported (53, 54). This supports the utility of our approach, as these genes, while clearly associated with other monogenic conditions, appear to also be involved in KSD, probably through secondary effects such as dysregulation of calcium and phosphate metabolism by PHEX, GNA11 or FGF23 mutations.

Two of the newly nominated genes, namely MUC2 and MUC20, are on Exomiser's black list due to having a high number of variants called in healthy individuals. Since having a kidney stone is not a typical exclusion criterium when recruiting healthy control participants in most studies and since there is already some evidence for the involvement of another mucin gene (MUC1) in KSD (55,56), we decided not to exclude these genes from the nominated list.

To further explore the plausibility of an association between KSD and the candidate genes nominated by Exomiser, we next investigated if we could identify some of these novel nominated genes through other methods.

Comparing Exomiser-nominated genes with gene-level rare variant enrichment

As an orthogonal approach for identification of novel candidate genes for monogenic KSD, we performed a gene-level rare variant enrichment analysis to identify KSD-candidate genes in the SKSC. To improve statistical power, we increased the number of control samples by including WES data from in-house controls sequenced in the same manner (N = 621).

Unfortunately, no gene reached genome-wide significance for KS association in the genelevel analysis (Suppl. Figure 2), which is not surprising given the limited sample size.

However, 2 out of the 62 newly nominated genes through Exomiser reached nominal significance in this gene-level rare variant enrichment analysis (p < 0.05): NCF1 and ABCC6 (Suppl. Table 4 and Suppl. Figure 3). Both of these are known disease genes, where bi-allelic pathogenic variants in NCF1 cause chronic granulomatosis disease while bi-allelic pathogenic variants in ABCC6 are responsible for pseudoxanthoma elasticum. Both disorders are inherited in a recessive manner. In pseudoxanthoma elasticum, ABCC6 dysfunction leads to reduced ATP transport and decreased levels of the circulating calcification inhibitor PPi, which in turn causes abnormal tissue calcifications including formation of kidney stones in some patients (57).

In an independent approach, we also utilized the UK Biobank data for gene-level enrichment in individuals with KS. This identified 6 of the Exomiser-nominated genes that reached nominal significance (p < 0.05) (Suppl. Table 4), among which we found again ABCC6. An overview of the overlap of nominated genes that were found by the gene-level approaches (at least on a nominal level) is provided in Figure 3B. Of note, ABCC6 was the only gene significantly associated with KS in both the SKSC and the UK Biobank sample (SKSC: p = 0.007; UK Biobank: p = 0.0005). We therefore focused on this gene for further exploration.

We next manually classified all rare (MAF < 0.01), exonic ABCC6 variants in the SKSC according to the ACMG criteria. 80 individuals had an ABCC6 variant, of which 31 harbored one likely pathogenic/pathogenic (LP/P) variant, 10 a likely benign/benign (LB/B) and 41 a variant of unknown significance (VUS). All but one individual were heterozygous for the LP/P ABCC6 variants. Two individuals had two variants each, the first carrying a P and a VUS variant, and the second carrying a VUS and a B variant (whereby the phase cannot be established here based on WES data alone). There were 10 unique LP/P variants, reported in Table 1. Importantly, LP/P variants in ABCC6 were significantly more prevalent in KSF than in CT-confirmed NKSF (OR = 8.9, p = 0.007). Two out of the ten variants of interest were ranked top 1 by Exomiser. All ABCC6 variants, including VUS and LB/B variants are reported in Suppl. Table 6.

For LP/P ABCC6 variants with MAF > 0.001 we additionally checked for a variant-level kidney stone association in the UK Biobank. This identified two such variants, both with significant kidney stone association (NM_001171.6: c.3421C>T: OR = 2.01, p = 0.0006; NM_001171.6: c.1171A>G: OR = 1.42, p = 0.002), Suppl. Table 7.

We next analyzed the clinical and biochemical data in a cohort of individuals with heterozygous LP/P ABCC6 variants (N=159) from Belgium. 15.72% (25/159) of individuals had renal calcifications and/or clinical episode(s) of lithiasis. Since the precise prevalence of KSD and of renal calcifications is unknown in this population, it remains unclear whether this represents a significantly increased incidence. Analysis of the plasma PPi levels in heterozygous LP/P ABCC6 variant carriers did not show a significant difference between individuals with or without a history of kidney stones (Suppl. Figure S4). Despite this, the genetic association between LP/P ABCC6 variants identified through our Exomiser approach is supported by the gene-level rare variant enrichment analysis in the SKSC and in UK biobank, by the variant-level association in the UK biobank and by previous literature (57, 58).

Discussion

This study shows how a widely used tool for variant prioritization developed for rare diseases can be used for identifying monogenic forms of a common, complex disease. The availability of a large and carefully curated dataset, where genetic variant interpretation is supported by biochemical data, represents an ideal setting for benchmarking Exomiser in the context of a common disease. After optimizing the settings for our purpose by extending the phenotypic list and disregarding previously assigned inheritance modes, 94% of the "gold standard" gene-participant pairings were prioritized by Exomiser within the top 5 rankings, indicating good performance. Since inclusion of variants ranked below 5 did not substantially increase the performance, rank 5 may be an optimal cutoff in the context of (this) common disease, where carefully balancing the signal-to-noise ratio is particularly important due to the expectation that the majority of participants are not affected by monogenic forms of the disease.

We further extended this pipeline to utilize Exomiser for novel gene discovery and nominated 62 genes not previously considered causative for monogenic KSD as potentially relevant for kidney stones. Interestingly, several of these genes have already been tentatively associated with KSD (52), serving as a positive control for our approach and indicating that we can successfully identify relevant signals by "casting a wider net". This is further supported by the orthogonal approach relying on gene-level enrichment analysis in the SKSC and the UK Biobank, which both identified the adenosine triphosphate (ATP) binding cassette subfamily C member 6 (ABCC6) as associated with KSD. ABCC6 is a transmembrane protein predominantly expressed in the liver and the kidney (59).

Mutations in this gene are linked to low levels of plasma PPi, an inhibitor of calcium crystallization, and have been associated with two rare diseases: generalized arterial calcification of infancy (GACI) (60) and pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) (61). PXE is an autosomal recessive multisystem rare genetic disorder characterized by elastic fiber calcification in the skin, the cardiovascular system, and the eyes, and has also been previously associated with an increased KSD risk (57, (62) (63) (64). Heterozygous ABCC6 mutations have also been reported in individuals with recurrent KSD (58) and linked to kidney stone occurrence as part of a large population copy number variation analysis (65). Therefore, this gene is indeed considered as a strong candidate risk factor for KSD and prioritizing it by an exome-wide automated search may be seen as a proof of principle for utilization of this methodology for identification of genes linked to monogenic forms of common diseases. This study illustrates the potential utility of automated variant prioritization for the investigation of monogenic forms of common diseases. This approach can now also be applied to identify monogenic forms of other common diseases in large cohorts, where its performance should be tested. Indeed, some limitations must be taken into account, as is the case with all automated approaches but particularly in the context of common diseases.

As with a lot of genetic data, a good gold standard dataset for benchmarking is hard to obtain, since it is often difficult to prove the pathogenicity of genetic variants without functional studies. In this study, we could take advantage of deep phenotypic information including biochemical data to support our interpretation of the effects of variants (21).

Generating a reliable gold standard dataset for benchmarking can however represent a challenge in other disorders where biochemical data are not available or as relevant.

Applying the Exomiser settings defined here without disorder-specific benchmarking may be of value but would require some positive controls in the dataset to evaluate the overall performance. A major challenge in this context is the uncertainty about the actual proportion of monogenic cases in various common diseases, which directly influences the MAF cut-offs for Exomiser. This is also linked to the fact that incomplete penetrance is frequent in monogenic cases of common diseases and that disease may manifest later in life. Consequently, controls may carry strong disease risk alleles. In this case, we estimated based on previous work that approximately 10% of KSD may be of or close to monogenic nature with a strong risk factor in one gene. Since the overall prevalence of KSD is around 10%, this allowed us to determine a MAF cut-off of 1% (10% of 10%). This would certainly need to be adapted to each disorder group based on current disease prevalence data.

One limitation of our study is that the majority of participants in the SKSC were of European ancestry. Therefore, how these findings translate to other ancestries remains to be systematically investigated in future studies. Moreover, here we only focused on coding variants using WES. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) and utilizing Genomiser (a variant prioritization tool including non-coding regions) has been suggested as a second step for WES-undiagnosed individuals in rare diseases (33). Given the difficulty in interpreting the significance of non-coding variants even in rare monogenic diseases, this may prove to be even more challenging in the context of rare monogenic forms of common disease, where the proportion of expected monogenic cases is unclear. Finally, while the use of Exomiser is well-established in the context of Mendelian diseases, it is not the only tool available. The choice for rare variant prioritization software is rapidly growing (10, 11, (66) (67) (68), and it remains to be seen how the performance of other automated tools will compare in the context of KSD and other common diseases.

In summary, we systematically investigated the use of automated variant prioritization with Exomiser in a large KSD cohort, as an example for a common disease with monogenic forms.

With the optimal approach, Exomiser ranked within the top five rankings nearly all previously defined "gold standard" KSD gene-participant pairs from an established KSD gene panel. Using this tool, we additionally nominated novel genes which are now available to the scientific community for further investigation (https://sksc-variant-and-biochemistry.shinyapps.io/exomiser-candidates/). Using orthogonal approaches, we present ABCC6 as an example of a strong KSD candidate gene, also in line with previous research.

Therefore, this study may serve as an example of automated variant prioritization in the context of monogenic forms of common diseases which is a key step for precision medicine, given its potentially high clinical utility. In the case of KSD, we could previously show that having a rare genetic variant with a strong impact in KSD-related genes is predictive of kidney stone recurrence (21) which may impact the clinical management of affected individuals. With this study, we take a step further toward the successful diagnosis of monogenic forms of common diseases, with potential impact on disease prognosis and treatment. 511 An overview of the data analyses workflow. The lack of significant association between plasma PPi levels and history of kidney stones in an independent cohort of heterozygous ABCC6 carriers reported in this study does not exclude an effect for heterozygous LP/P ABCC6 variants acting as risk factors for KSD. The small number of individuals limits statistical power and it remains uncertain how much a single plasma PPi measurement is representative of tissue-relevant levels, e.g., urine or kidney levels. Given the converging genetic evidence for ABCC6 involvement in KSD through Exomiser, rare variant enrichment analyses in the SKSC cohort and the UK Biobank, as well as previous reports, it appears likely that LP/P variants in this gene represent a strong risk factor, and place ABCC6-associated KSD towards the "monogenic with incomplete penetrance" end of the disease spectrum.

The initial cutoff score for results filtering is depicted as a gray dashed line, and the cutoff deemed as optimal as a green dashed line (in case they overlap, only the green line is seen). The error bars represent the standard deviation from the mean. (C) Overview of Exomiser's automated variant classification based on ACMG criteria per variant-participant pairing within "non-established" (in blue) and established genes (in red), respectively. The numbers indicate the number of variants in each ACMG category. As expected, for non-established genes, where all variants were considered for ranking, all ACMG categories (P, LP, VUS, LB, B) are represented while for the established genes the variants preselected for disease relevance (gold standard) do not include LB/B variants.
